title: Culture Is What You Do, Not What You Say
author: Molly Graham
summary: Molly Graham, former Facebook HR executive, uses a conversation with Mike Schroepfer (Facebook's longtime CTO) to articulate three core beliefs about organizational culture. Culture comes from the top — specifically from the founder's personality and behavior, not from HR exercises or values statements. What you do matters more than what you write down — culture is the behavior of senior leaders, and there is always a culture even in organizations that have never articulated one. And culture must evolve as organizations grow. The article's most striking moment is Schroepfer's story about a worldwide Facebook outage: when someone raised their hand mid-crisis and said 'I think it was my diff that took the site down,' the reaction was zero blame and a focus on recovery. Graham argues that kind of safety is not built by policy but by a thousand small behavioral decisions about who gets celebrated, how failures are examined, and what the leader actually does in the room — not what they say they value.
points: Culture is not built from the bottom up: it is a direct reflection of the founder's personality and behavior, reinforced and reverberated by senior leaders. HR cultural exercises that are not grounded in and aligned with the founder's actual behavior cannot substitute for the real thing.

The largest gap in most organizations is not between stated values and actual values but between what leaders say and what leaders do. When that gap widens, it creates distraction and demoralization that is extraordinarily hard to close.

Schroepfer's outage story is the article's central proof: when someone volunteers to take blame for a disaster in front of their boss's boss, it is because every prior behavioral signal from leadership made it safe to do so. That safety is the product of hundreds of small decisions, not a single policy.

Choosing where to work is choosing a personality to work inside of. Senior leaders in particular need to study the founder's character carefully, because they will spend their careers translating that character into organizational behavior.

The cultural artifacts companies produce — values documents, posters, training programs — are attempts to articulate a culture that already exists. They work when they accurately describe what the top is already doing; they fail when they describe an aspiration at odds with daily behavior.
quotes: The vast majority of culture is shaped by the personality and behaviors of the founder. After that, it's reinforced and reverberated by the senior leaders around them. 'Most cultures are a direct reflection of the founder. It's really hard to build a company culture with an involved founder that's orthogonal to how the founder feels.'

You could never write anything down — no values, no posters, no principles — and you would still have a culture. Culture is crafted through the behavior of the people at the top. Your culture already exists; you just have to figure out how to articulate it.

When there is dissonance between what you say and what you do, people get lost. You say you value bottoms-up feedback, but you fire people who give it. You say you want transparency, but you make decisions behind closed doors. The larger that gap, the more distracting and demoralizing it is for everyone inside it.

Think about what it takes to say that. In the middle of a disaster. In front of your boss's boss. When people are already stressed and losing money and looking for answers. The only way that happens is if the person raising their hand already know what's coming next.

What happened next at Facebook was: zero blaming. Zero yelling. 'Thank you. You got us back up faster. Now let's figure out how this never happens again.' That safety wasn't built by a policy or a values statement. It was built by a thousand small decisions.
When you're choosing where to work, you're basically choosing a personality to work inside of, weird as that might sound. The more senior you get, the more carefully you need to think about that.
